etymology: Named in honor of the Front Populaire (Popular Front), the coalition of left-wing parties that governed France from 1936 to 1938 under Leon Blum. The coalition implemented significant social reforms including the 40-hour work week, paid holidays, and collective bargaining agreements, transforming French labor law.

name: Aimé Césaire
etymology: Named after Aime Cesaire (1913-2008), a Martinican poet, author, and politician who was one of the founders of the Negritude literary movement alongside Leopold Sedar Senghor. He served as mayor of Fort-de-France for over 50 years and as a deputy in the French National Assembly, and his works explored the legacy of colonialism and the African diaspora.

name: Mairie d'Issy
etymology: Named after the town hall (mairie) of Issy-les-Moulineaux, a commune in the Hauts-de-Seine department southwest of Paris. The name 'Issy' derives from the Gallo-Roman estate name Isciacum. The commune is also known for the Seminaire d'Issy, where significant theological conferences took place in the 17th century.

name: Corentin Celton
etymology: Originally named Petits Menages after the nearby hospice. Renamed on 15 October 1945 in honor of Corentin Celton (1901-1943), an employee at the Hospice des Petits Menages and a member of the French Resistance. He was arrested for distributing clandestine literature and was executed by the Nazis at Mont-Valerien.

name: Porte de Versailles
etymology: Named after one of the gates in the Thiers fortification wall of Paris, which led toward the city of Versailles to the southwest. The area is best known for the Parc des Expositions de la Porte de Versailles, one of the largest exhibition centers in Europe, which has hosted major trade fairs and events since 1923.

name: Convention
etymology: Named after the Rue de la Convention, which commemorates the Convention nationale (National Convention), the revolutionary assembly that governed France from 1792 to 1795. The Convention abolished the monarchy, proclaimed the First French Republic, and oversaw the trial and execution of King Louis XVI.

name: Vaugirard
etymology: Named after the Rue de Vaugirard, the longest street in Paris at over four kilometers. The name derives from the former village of Vaugirard (originally Val Boitron, then Val Gerard, and eventually Vaugirard), which was an independent commune until its annexation by Paris in 1860.

name: Volontaires
etymology: Named after the Rue des Volontaires, which honors the volunteers (volontaires) who enlisted in the French Revolutionary armies during the wars of the First French Republic in the 1790s. These citizen-soldiers responded to the levee en masse decreed by the Convention nationale in 1793 to defend France against the European monarchies.

name: Falguière
etymology: Named after the Rue Falguiere, honoring Alexandre Falguiere (1831-1900), a French sculptor and painter from Toulouse. He won the Prix de Rome in 1859 and became one of the most celebrated sculptors of the Third Republic, creating notable works including the allegorical group on the Arc de Triomphe and numerous public monuments.

name: Notre-Dame-des-Champs
etymology: Named after the Rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs, which refers to a medieval priory and church dedicated to the Virgin Mary 'of the fields' (des champs). The priory of Notre-Dame-des-Champs was founded in the 6th century on the site of a former pagan temple and stood in what were then the rural outskirts of Paris.

name: Rennes
etymology: Named after the Rue de Rennes, which takes its name from the city of Rennes, the capital of Brittany in northwestern France. The street was laid out in the mid-19th century as part of a planned boulevard intended to connect the Gare Montparnasse to the Seine, though the project was never fully completed.

name: Sèvres - Babylone
etymology: Named after the intersection of the Rue de Sevres and the Rue de Babylone. The Rue de Sevres leads toward the town of Sevres, known for its porcelain manufactory. The Rue de Babylone takes its name from a corruption of 'Babel-Orient,' referring to the seminary of the Missions Etrangeres (Foreign Missions) located on the street.

name: Rue du Bac
etymology: Named after the Rue du Bac, one of the principal streets of the 7th arrondissement. The word 'bac' means ferry, referring to a flat-bottomed boat that once crossed the Seine at this location to transport stone blocks for the construction of the Palais des Tuileries in the 16th century.

name: Solférino
etymology: Named after the Rue de Solferino, which commemorates the Battle of Solferino fought on 24 June 1859 in Lombardy, Italy. In this decisive engagement of the Second Italian War of Independence, the Franco-Sardinian alliance defeated the Austrian Empire. The battle's carnage also inspired Henry Dunant to found the Red Cross.

name: Assemblée Nationale
etymology: Named after the Assemblee nationale, the lower house of the French Parliament, which meets in the Palais Bourbon on the Left Bank of the Seine. The station was originally named Chambre des Deputes after the pre-war legislative body and was renamed Assemblee nationale in 1989 during the bicentennial of the French Revolution.

name: Trinité - d'Estienne d'Orves
etymology: Named after the Eglise de la Sainte-Trinite, a 19th-century church dedicated to the Holy Trinity, and the Place d'Estienne d'Orves. The square honors Honore d'Estienne d'Orves (1901-1941), a French naval officer and one of the first members of the Free French Forces who was captured by the Gestapo and executed at Mont-Valerien.

name: Notre-Dame-de-Lorette
etymology: Named after the Eglise Notre-Dame-de-Lorette, a neoclassical basilica completed in 1836 and dedicated to Our Lady of Loreto. The church references the Holy House of Loreto in Italy, where according to Catholic tradition the house of the Virgin Mary was miraculously transported from Nazareth by angels in the 13th century.

name: Saint-Georges
etymology: Named after the Place Saint-Georges, a small square in the 9th arrondissement. The square takes its name from a chapel dedicated to Saint George that once stood in the area. The Place Saint-Georges is notable for its central fountain and for being the location of the Fondation Dosne-Thiers, a library and museum.

name: Abbesses
etymology: Named after the Rue des Abbesses, which refers to the abbesses who governed the Benedictine Abbey of Montmartre, founded in 1133 by King Louis VI and Queen Adelaide of Savoy. The abbey was one of the most important religious institutions on the Butte Montmartre until its dissolution during the French Revolution.

name: Lamarck - Caulaincourt
etymology: Named after the intersection of the Rue Lamarck and the Rue Caulaincourt. Jean-Baptiste Lamarck (1744-1829) was a pioneering French naturalist who developed an early theory of biological evolution. Armand de Caulaincourt (1773-1827) was a French general and diplomat who served as Napoleon's ambassador to Russia and later as Foreign Minister.

name: Jules Joffrin
etymology: Named after the Rue Jules Joffrin, honoring Jules Joffrin (1846-1890), a French socialist politician and municipal councillor of the 18th arrondissement. A former metalworker and trade unionist, he was a prominent advocate for workers' rights and was elected to the Paris Municipal Council, where he championed social reforms until his early death.

name: Marx Dormoy
etymology: Originally named Torcy after the nearby Place de Torcy. Renamed on 11 May 1946 in honor of Marx Dormoy (1888-1941), a French socialist politician who served as Minister of the Interior under Leon Blum's Popular Front government. He was assassinated by the far-right Cagoule organization using a time bomb in his hotel room in Montelimar.

name: Porte de la Chapelle
etymology: Named after one of the gates in the Thiers fortification wall of Paris, which led to the village of La Chapelle. The name refers to a medieval chapel (chapelle) dedicated to various saints that once stood in the area. La Chapelle was an independent commune that was annexed by Paris in 1860 as part of the 18th arrondissement.

name: Châtillon - Montrouge
etymology: Named after the communes of Châtillon and Montrouge in the southern suburbs of Paris. Châtillon derives from the Latin 'castellum' meaning small fortress, while Montrouge means 'red hill,' likely referring to the reddish clay soil found in the area. The station serves as the southern terminus of Line 13.

name: Malakoff - Plateau de Vanves
etymology: Named after the commune of Malakoff and the Plateau de Vanves neighborhood. Malakoff was named after the Tour Malakoff, a tower built by a local tavern owner to commemorate the French capture of the Malakoff redoubt during the Siege of Sevastopol in 1855 during the Crimean War. Vanves derives from the Gallo-Roman personal name Vanedia.

name: Malakoff - Rue Étienne Dolet
etymology: Named after the Rue Étienne Dolet in the commune of Malakoff. Étienne Dolet (1509-1546) was a French scholar, translator, and printer who was a prominent figure of the Renaissance. He was convicted of heresy and blasphemy and was strangled and burned at the stake on Place Maubert in Paris.

name: Porte de Vanves
etymology: Named after the Porte de Vanves, one of the gates in the Thiers fortification wall built around Paris in the 1840s. The gate led to the commune of Vanves, whose name derives from a Gallo-Roman estate. The area is known for its weekend flea market, one of the most popular in Paris.

name: Plaisance
etymology: Named after the Rue de Plaisance and the surrounding Plaisance neighborhood in the 14th arrondissement. The name means 'pleasure' or 'pleasant place' in French and was given to this area when it was developed as a residential quarter in the mid-19th century. The neighborhood was historically home to a working-class community.

name: Pernety
etymology: Named after the Rue Pernety, which honors Antoine-Joseph Pernety (1716-1801), a French Benedictine monk, writer, and explorer. He accompanied Louis Antoine de Bougainville on his expedition to the Falkland Islands in 1763-1764 and published an account of the voyage. He later became librarian to Frederick the Great of Prussia.

name: Gaîté
etymology: Named after the Rue de la Gaîté, a street in the 14th arrondissement known since the 18th century for its theaters, cabarets, and entertainment venues. The name means 'gaiety' or 'merriment' in French. The street has hosted numerous theaters including the Théâtre de la Gaîté-Montparnasse and the Bobino music hall.

name: Duroc
etymology: Named after the Boulevard des Invalides and nearby Place Duroc, which honor Géraud Christophe Michel Duroc, 1st Duke of Friuli (1772-1813). Duroc was a French general and diplomat who served as Napoleon's Grand Marshal of the Palace. He was killed by a cannonball at the Battle of Bautzen during the Napoleonic Wars.

name: Saint-François-Xavier
etymology: Named after the nearby Church of Saint-François-Xavier, built between 1861 and 1874 by architect Joseph-Ulysse Lelong. The church is dedicated to Saint Francis Xavier (1506-1552), a Spanish Jesuit missionary and co-founder of the Society of Jesus, who is the patron saint of missionaries. He evangelized extensively in Asia, particularly in India, Japan, and the East Indies.

name: Varenne
etymology: Named after the Rue de Varenne, one of the most prestigious streets in the 7th arrondissement. The name derives from 'garenne,' an old French term meaning a game preserve or rabbit warren, referring to the hunting grounds that once occupied this area. The Hôtel Matignon, official residence of the French Prime Minister, and the Musée Rodin are both located on this street.

name: Miromesnil
etymology: Named after the Rue de Miromesnil, which honors Armand Thomas Hue de Miromesnil (1723-1796), who served as Keeper of the Seals of France under Louis XVI from 1774 to 1787. He was a moderate reformer who opposed some of the more radical proposals of Turgot and Necker. The street runs through the fashionable 8th arrondissement.

name: Liège
etymology: Originally named Berlin when it opened in 1911, reflecting the nearby Rue de Berlin. At the outbreak of World War I in August 1914, the station was renamed Liège in honor of the Belgian city that heroically resisted the German invasion. The Battle of Liège in August 1914 was one of the first engagements of the war. The station is decorated with ceramic panels depicting scenes from Liège.

name: La Fourche
etymology: Named after the fork ('fourche') in the road where the Avenue de Saint-Ouen and the Avenue de Clichy diverge. This is also the point where Line 13 splits into its two northern branches, one heading to Saint-Denis and the other to Asnières-Gennevilliers, making the station name doubly appropriate.

name: Guy Môquet
etymology: Originally named Carrefour Nollet after a nearby crossroads. Renamed in 1946 in honor of Guy Môquet (1924-1941), a young French Communist resistance figure who was arrested for distributing anti-German leaflets. He was executed by the Nazis at age 17 as one of the hostages shot at Châteaubriant in reprisal for the assassination of a German officer.

name: Porte de Saint-Ouen
etymology: Named after the Porte de Saint-Ouen, one of the gates in the Thiers fortification wall of Paris. The gate opened onto the road leading to Saint-Ouen, a commune named after Saint Audoenus (Ouen), a 7th-century bishop of Rouen and chancellor to King Dagobert I. The area was historically part of the Zone, the military non-building zone surrounding the fortifications.

name: Garibaldi
etymology: Named after the Boulevard Garibaldi in Saint-Ouen, which honors Giuseppe Garibaldi (1807-1882), the Italian general and nationalist who was a central figure in the unification of Italy. Garibaldi also fought for France during the Franco-Prussian War of 1870-1871, commanding the Army of the Vosges as a volunteer.

name: Mairie de Saint-Ouen
etymology: Named after the town hall (mairie) of Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine. The commune of Saint-Ouen takes its name from Saint Audoenus (Ouen in French), a 7th-century bishop of Rouen who served as chancellor and referendary to the Merovingian kings Clotaire II and Dagobert I. The Line 14 extension to this station opened on 24 June 2020.

name: Porte de Clichy
etymology: Named after the Porte de Clichy, one of the gates in the Thiers fortification wall of Paris built in the 1840s. The gate opened onto the road leading to the commune of Clichy, whose name derives from the Gallo-Roman estate 'Clippiacum.' The Line 14 extension to this station opened on 14 December 2020.

name: Brochant
etymology: Named after the Rue Brochant, which honors André Jean Marie Brochant de Villiers (1772-1840), a French geologist and mineralogist. He was a professor at the École des Mines and a member of the Académie des Sciences. He directed the creation of the first geological map of France and was an important figure in the development of French geology.

name: Saint-Denis - Porte de Paris
etymology: Named after the commune of Saint-Denis and the Porte de Paris, a triumphal arch built in 1672 by architect Michel Villedo to commemorate the victories of Louis XIV along the Rhine. Saint-Denis takes its name from the first bishop of Paris, who was martyred around 250 AD. According to legend, after his decapitation he carried his own head to the site of the future basilica.

name: Basilique de Saint-Denis
etymology: Named after the Basilica of Saint-Denis, one of the most important Gothic churches in France and the burial site of nearly every French monarch from the 10th to the 18th century. The basilica was built on the grave of Saint Denis, the patron saint of France, and its reconstruction under Abbot Suger around 1135-1144 is considered the origin of Gothic architecture.

name: Les Courtilles
etymology: Named after the Les Courtilles neighborhood on the border of Asnières-sur-Seine and Gennevilliers. The word 'courtille' is an old French term derived from the Latin 'cortis' meaning a small enclosed garden or courtyard, referring to the market gardens that once occupied this area. The station is the northwestern terminus of Line 13.

name: Les Agnettes
etymology: Named after the Les Agnettes neighborhood at the border of Asnières-sur-Seine and Gennevilliers. The name likely derives from 'agneau' (lamb), suggesting the area was historically used for sheep grazing or had a connection to the wool trade. The neighborhood sits on elevated ground above the Seine flood plain.

name: Gabriel Péri
etymology: Named after Gabriel Péri (1902-1941), a French Communist politician and journalist who served as a member of the Chamber of Deputies. He was head of the foreign affairs section of the newspaper L'Humanité. Arrested by the Vichy police in 1941 and handed over to the Germans, he was executed by firing squad at Mont-Valérien on 15 December 1941.

name: Bibliothèque François Mitterrand
etymology: Named after the Bibliothèque nationale de France site François-Mitterrand, the main building of France's national library. Designed by architect Dominique Perrault and inaugurated in 1996, the library's four glass towers evoke open books. It was named after President François Mitterrand (1916-1996), who initiated the project in 1988 as one of his grands travaux to modernize Paris.

name: Olympiades
etymology: Named after the Les Olympiades urban development complex, a large elevated pedestrian platform built in the early 1970s in the 13th arrondissement. The complex and its surrounding towers were named after various Olympic Games host cities (Athens, Helsinki, Mexico, etc.). The area is the heart of Paris's Chinatown neighborhood.

name: Saint-Denis - Pleyel
etymology: Named after the commune of Saint-Denis and the Pleyel neighborhood, which takes its name from Ignace Pleyel (1757-1831), an Austrian-French composer and piano manufacturer. Pleyel founded the Pleyel piano company and its factory was located in Saint-Denis. The Salle Pleyel concert hall in Paris was also named after him. The station opened as part of the Line 14 northern extension for the 2024 Paris Olympics.

name: Aéroport d'Orly
etymology: Named after Paris-Orly Airport, the second-busiest airport in France after Charles de Gaulle. The airport takes its name from the commune of Orly, derived from the Gallo-Roman name 'Aureliacum,' referring to an estate belonging to someone named Aurelius. The station opened as part of the Line 14 southern extension for the 2024 Paris Olympics, providing a direct metro link to the airport.

name: Pont Cardinet
etymology: Named after the Pont Cardinet, a bridge that crosses the railway tracks of the Gare Saint-Lazare in the 17th arrondissement. The bridge and nearby street are named after Jean Cardinet (1751-1818), a local landowner and mayor of the former commune of Les Batignolles. The area was historically associated with the Batignolles railway yards.
